title: What's the difference between infrastructure as code and configuration management?
description: Declarative provisioning vs imperative configuration — Terraform/ARM/Bicep vs Ansible/Chef, how they fit together, and why the distinction matters for repeatable environments.

data.text: Question: What's the difference between infrastructure as code and configuration management?

Infrastructure as code (IaC) provisions the infrastructure itself — VMs, networks, managed databases — declaratively describing the desired end state (Terraform, ARM/Bicep, Pulumi). Configuration management installs and sets up software *on* that infrastructure — web servers, runtimes, agents — often idempotently and repeatedly (Ansible, Chef, DSC). IaC creates the machine; configuration management makes the machine useful. In cloud-native stacks, containers and managed services shrink config management's role, but the principle — converge reality toward a declared state — is shared.

items: IaC: describes resources via a plan/apply cycle — Terraform plans a diff against state, then applies it; the state file is the source of truth for what exists
Idempotency is the core guarantee: re-running converges toward the declared state without duplicating resources
Config management: runs on already-provisioned hosts, installing packages, writing configs, starting services — Ansible is agentless (SSH/WinRM), Chef uses an agent + recipes
Separation of concerns: IaC is per-environment (dev/stage/prod); config management is per-role (web, worker, db)
Modern convergence: Pulumi blurs the line by using real languages for IaC; container images bake config in, so config management mostly manages the platform, not each VM
Drift is the enemy both fight: a hand-changed cloud resource or a manually patched server — detect it, then re-apply instead of trusting the manual fix

data.code:
# --- Infrastructure as code (Terraform): the resource itself ---
resource "azurerm_sql_server" "app" {
  name                         = "app-sql-${var.env}"
  resource_group_name          = azurerm_resource_group.app.name
  location                     = azurerm_resource_group.app.location
  version                      = "12.0"
  administrator_login          = var.sql_admin
  administrator_login_password = var.sql_password
}

# terraform plan  -> shows the diff vs state
# terraform apply -> creates/updates to match

# --- Configuration management (Ansible): software ON the host ---
- name: Configure web server
  hosts: web
  tasks:
    - ansible.builtin.apt:
        name: [dotnet-runtime-9.0, nginx]
        state: present
    - ansible.builtin.template:
        src: nginx.conf.j2
        dest: /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/app.conf
    - ansible.builtin.systemd:
        name: nginx
        state: restarted
        enabled: true

data.title: Where the line is moving
data.text: With PaaS, containers, and serverless, you rarely configure a VM directly — the platform is the runtime. That shifts 'configuration' into code and images (Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests) and leaves IaC to provision the managed services those run on. The vocabulary blurs, but the habit of declaring desired state and converging to it stays.

items: Treating the Terraform state file carelessly — it holds secrets and can't be casually edited
Mixing provisioning and configuration in one unmaintainable script
Hand-editing resources in the cloud console, creating drift the next apply reverts
Committing secrets into IaC files instead of using a key vault or secret store
Assuming config management is obsolete — it still matters for the platform layer

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: IaC provisions infrastructure; config management sets up software on it
Both are declarative and idempotent — converge toward declared state
IaC is per-environment; config management is per-role
Fight drift: re-apply, don't trust the manual fix
data.takeaway: IaC creates the machine, config management makes it useful — and both exist so reality matches a version-controlled declaration.
